headline: Race Point on the ebb: mackerel schools pull bass up, cod holding tight off Billingsgate
subhead: A calm week on the Bay — bass and blues stacked on bait at Race Point, cod still there if you find the right piece of bottom off Billingsgate.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, an hour before the top of the ebb off Race Point, the sounder with a school of mackerel sitting at 35 feet, tight and nervous, the way they get when something's underneath them. I dropped a rod with a live mack down through the school on a fish-finder rig, no weight to speak of, just let the current do the work. Didn't take thirty seconds before the rod bent hard and stayed bent. Twenty-six pound bass, fat and bright, came up thrashing in that green rip water where the outgoing tide runs against the shoal. That's been the story all week out there — find the mackerel, and the bass aren't far behind.

The rip off Race Point has been holding up the way it does this time of year, best from the last two hours of the ebb into the slack, working the seam where the deeper water — 30 to 45 feet — meets the shallower bar. We've been drifting live mackerel and whole squid on fish-finder rigs, letting the boat set the pace rather than working the reel. Bass have run 20 to 30 pounds mixed with a good number of schoolies, and there's enough of a push of bigger fish in there that a few boats have had 30-plus pound bass on umbrella rigs trolled slow along the edge where the rip flattens out. Peaked Hill Bars, just south, has had bluefish mixed into the same water — sand eels showing on top, birds working, blues in the 4 to 8 pound class hitting metal, Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters worked fast through the froth.

We called this one last week — said stable conditions would hold through the week, and they have. Light southwest wind, no real chop to speak of, and that's kept the rip fishing consistent rather than the boom-and-bust you get when a blow stirs up the bottom. Cape Cod Bay is still running cooler than the Sound and Buzzards Bay right now, and that's the whole ballgame up here — while stripers down south are getting pushed deep and nocturnal by warm surface water, our bass are still willing to feed in daylight on structure because the Gulf of Maine keeps this water in a range they like. It won't last forever, but for now, it's working in our favor.

Cod have been a different story — there, but you have to earn it. Billingsgate shoals, out in 55 to 70 feet on the drop-offs east of the flats, has given up a handful of decent cod, 8 to 15 pounds, on diamond jigs tipped with squid strips, worked right on the bottom during the slack water when the drift slows enough to keep the jig down where it belongs. It's not the kind of bite where you fill a cooler — some drifts we marked fish and never got a bite, others we boated three keepers in twenty minutes. The cod are there, holding tight to specific humps and ledges rather than spread out, and if you're not sitting right on the structure with your sounder, you're just burning gas. I'd rather make five short, precise drifts over the right piece of bottom than one long drift over nothing.

Fluke fishing has been the more dependable program if you want a full box without the guesswork. Barnstable Harbor's channel edges and the flats off Sandy Neck have been giving up keeper fluke in the 18 to 22 inch range, mixed with plenty of shorts, on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the outgoing as warm water drains out of the marsh creeks. That warm water pouring off the flats pushes bait — and the fluke — right to the channel edges, and a slow drag along that seam has been more productive than working the open flat itself. Brewster's flats, on the low side of the tide, have had a few stray fluke too, though that bite's thinner than Barnstable.

The moon's building back toward the new moon on the 12th, and the tides are starting to swing a little harder than the dead-flat neaps we had midweek. That's going to sharpen up the rip at Race Point — more current means a tighter, more defined edge for the bass and bluefish to work, and I expect the mackerel schools to hold there rather than scatter. If the pattern holds the way it has, I'd fish the two hours either side of the ebb at Race Point for bass and blues, and save the middle of the day for a run out to Billingsgate to work the cod on the slack. Keep an eye on the wind — if it swings around to the east and builds any real sea, the rip gets ugly fast and the drift turns into a chore instead of a pleasure. Barring that, this is a solid week to be out there, not a blowout, but honest fishing on a Bay that's still fishing the way it's supposed to in high summer.
